Neotoma cinerea exhibits a relatively low intrinsic rate of increase, reflecting its status as a comparatively slow-breeding rodent. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a body temperature of 37.8 °C [T = 37.8 °C], females typically produce litters containing 3.68 pups [N_R_i = litters containing 3.68 pups] per reproductive event. However, litters are produced infrequently, with an average of just under two litters per year [F_R_i = two litters per year], a rate that is modest compared to many small-bodied murid rodents. This reproductive strategy is consistent with a life history that prioritizes offspring quality and parental investment over high fecundity. Neonates are altricial and their initial mass is quite small; newborn pups weigh approximately 13.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 13.5 grams] at parturition, representing a minute fraction of the adult female's total mass. This low birth weight underscores the degree of altriciality in this species, as the young are entirely dependent on maternal care and lactation for the first several weeks of life.

The gestation period of the bushy-tailed woodrat is relatively prolonged compared to many cricetid rodents. Females carry their developing young for a gestation time of 30 days [tg = 30 days], a duration that is consistent with experimental measurements taken at a core body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. This comparatively lengthy gestation may be linked to the degree of neural development attained in utero, although the neonates are still born in an altricial state. Following parturition, the altricial young undergo a period of rapid somatic growth while relying exclusively on maternal milk. The time since birth at weaning is 27 days [tx = 27 days] when measured under standard thermal conditions at 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], after which the juveniles begin to consume solid food and become increasingly independent from the mother. This relatively short weaning period is typical of woodrats when compared to other rodents of similar body size.

The bushy-tailed woodrat achieves an impressive adult body size, with individuals reaching a maximum recorded wet weight of 335.5 grams [Wwi = 335.5 grams]. This ultimate wet weight is among the largest observed in the genus Neotoma and contributes to the species' reputation as a robust and stocky member of the packrat community. At the point of nutritional independence, the weanlings have already attained a substantial mass; the wet weight at weaning has been documented at 107 grams [Wwx = 107 grams]. This weight represents approximately one-third of the adult asymptotic mass, indicating that a considerable portion of juvenile growth occurs during the post-weaning subadult period. Field studies show that juveniles continue to gain mass steadily as they transition from milk to foraged vegetation, gradually approaching adult dimensions over the subsequent months. The disparity between weaning mass and adult mass highlights the importance of the juvenile growth phase in reaching reproductive size.

Sexual maturation in the bushy-tailed woodrat does not occur rapidly; instead, it follows a prolonged developmental trajectory consistent with the species' slow life history. Under basal metabolic conditions at a body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been recorded as 353 days [tp = 353 days]. This delayed onset of reproductive maturity, spanning nearly a full year, is markedly longer than that observed in many other cricetid rodents of comparable body size and likely reflects the need to acquire sufficient body condition to support the energetic costs of gestation and lactation. The protracted pubertal delay may be an adaptation to the relatively resource-limited environments the species inhabits, where early reproduction would impose a severe energetic burden on young females. This life-history pattern aligns with the classic "slow" end of the rodent fast-slow continuum, prioritizing survival and adult body size maintenance over precocious breeding.

Longevity data for the bushy-tailed woodrat, derived from comparative studies with the desert woodrat Neotoma lepida, indicate that this species can attain a considerable lifespan for a rodent of its mass. The maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at 10.5 years [am = 10.5 years], a figure obtained under standard thermal conditions at a body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. This remarkable longevity, surpassing a decade, is exceptionally long for a cricetid rodent and underscores the species' investment in somatic maintenance and survival over reproductive output. The link between a slow life history and extended lifespan is evident here: low annual fecundity, delayed maturity, and a long maximum lifespan form a coherent adaptive syndrome. In comparison with other small mammals, Neotoma cinerea stands out for its ability to persist across multiple years, allowing individuals to accumulate reproductive experience and contribute to population stability over time.
